pages.x: From the 1420s Portuguese ships, sent out by Prince Henry, called the Navigator, crept down the coast of Africa in small, nimble caravels. They were looking for gold, for slaves, and for a way round to the spices of Asia, which reached Europe only through Muslim and Venetian middlemen.

In 1488 Bartolomeu Dias was blown south by a storm for days. Turning east and finding no land, he sailed north and landed beyond the tip of Africa. His frightened crew made him turn back. He called it the Cape of Storms, but the king renamed it the Cape of Good Hope.

In 1497 Vasco da Gama swung far out into the Atlantic, rounded the Cape and, with a pilot found at Malindi, crossed the Indian Ocean on the monsoon winds. In May 1498 he reached Calicut. Asked what they had come for, his men answered: Christians and spices.

Of the 170 or so men who sailed with da Gama, only about 55 came home. Most were killed by scurvy, from a lack of fresh food. Even so, the pepper and spices he brought back paid for the voyage many times over.
The next fleet, under Pedro Álvares Cabral, swung so far west in 1500 that it struck an unknown coast: Brazil. Cabral claimed it for Portugal, sent a ship home with the news and sailed on to India.

In 1509 a Portuguese fleet with heavy guns destroyed the fleets of the Mamluk sultan of Egypt and of Gujarat off Diu, in India. For a century no one could match Portuguese guns at sea in the Indian Ocean.

Portugal could not conquer India, so it took the sea. Afonso de Albuquerque seized Goa in 1510, Malacca, the gateway to the spice islands, in 1511, and Hormuz, at the mouth of the Persian Gulf, in 1515. Ships trading without a Portuguese pass could be sunk.

The sea road joined Europe and Asia directly for the first time and began 450 years of European empires in Asia. Portugal held Goa until 1961 and Macau until 1999, and Portuguese is still spoken in Brazil, Angola and Mozambique.
